reason: Confirmed against the named edition. I downloaded the OCR text of the Boston Public Library copy myself (archive.org coplasdedonjorge00manr, dated 1833). Under the heading STANZAS, COMPOSED BY DON JORGE MANRIQUE ON THE DEATH OF HIS FATHER DON RODRIGO, stanza I reads: O let the soul her slumbers break, / Let thought be quickened, and awake, / Awake to see / How soon this life is past and gone, / And death comes softly stealing on, / How silently ! The words, the lineation and the line-head capitals match. It really is a comma after awake, as the verifier said, and the OCR space before the exclamation mark is period typesetting. Longfellow is the translator, 1833 is right, and so are stanza I and lines 1 to 6 of the twelve-line stanza. Coplas por la muerte de su padre is the standard name of the work. shipped.js: not shipped, no near opening, Manrique at 0 of 3, not banned. The poem is fifteenth-century Spanish, and neither it nor the translation is scripture or liturgy. It is in scope and publishable, and it suits the month exactly: an awakening to mortality, fit for six in the morning. The quotation ends on an exclamation mark, the verse is kept in lines, and the source leads with the name, carries no dash and runs to about 113 characters. Poetry is the right form.
